subject: Pathology
summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumour of the exocrine pancreas, most often in the head. It grows slowly, spreads early, and presents with vague abdominal pain and weight loss.

sections.p: PDAC is a malignant epithelial tumour arising from pancreatic ductal cells. Diagnosis requires imaging and histology. The tumour is usually hypovascular on CT and shows glandular structures on biopsy.

t.b: Tumour marker; elevated > 37 U/mL suggests PDAC but is not specific.
Provides tissue for cytology; confirms malignant ductal cells.
Defines tumour size, vascular involvement, and distant spread.

sections.p: The TNM system stages PDAC from I (localized) to IV (metastatic). Stage determines resectability and prognosis.
b: T: tumour size and local invasion

sections.p: Risk factors include smoking, chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, obesity, and genetic syndromes. Environmental toxins and diet also contribute.
Patients report dull epigastric pain radiating to the back, early satiety, weight loss, and sometimes jaundice if the tumour blocks the bile duct.
Work‑up combines imaging, tumour markers, and tissue diagnosis. In low‑resource settings, ultrasound and CA 19‑9 can guide referral.

t.b: Detects mass or biliary dilatation; limited sensitivity but useful where CT unavailable.
Elevated levels support diagnosis; normal does not exclude PDAC.
Staging and surgical planning; if unavailable, MRI is alternative.
Histology confirms adenocarcinoma; essential before treatment.

sections.p: Rapid weight loss, obstructive jaundice, new‑onset diabetes, or haemorrhage from tumour invasion are urgent signs.

Treatment follows tumour stage. Resectable disease gets surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy; unresectable disease receives palliative chemo or radiotherapy. Supportive care addresses pain and nutrition.
b: Nutrition – high‑protein diet and pancreatic enzyme supplements

sections.p: Regular imaging and CA 19‑9 monitoring detect recurrence. Prevention focuses on smoking cessation, weight control, and managing chronic pancreatitis.
Chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic pseudocyst, and neuroendocrine tumours can mimic PDAC clinically and on imaging.
b: Neuroendocrine tumour – usually hypervascular and hormonally active

sections.p: CA 19‑9 can be normal in early disease or elevated in benign biliary obstruction. Small tumours may be missed on ultrasound.
b: Ultrasound sensitivity – small head lesions may be invisible

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain, jaundice, unexplained weight loss, new‑onset diabetes, or haemorrhage

faq.q: Why is CA 19‑9 not a definitive test?
faq.a: It is sensitive but not specific; many benign conditions raise it, and some tumours do not produce it.
A low‑fat, high‑fiber diet and avoiding smoking reduce risk, but genetics also play a major role.

faq.q: What is the role of surgery?
faq.a: Surgery offers the only chance for cure in resectable disease, but most tumours are advanced by diagnosis.

exam: Explain the TNM staging of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and its impact on treatment options.
Describe the typical clinical presentation of a tumour in the head of the pancreas and why jaundice may occur.
Outline the first‑line chemotherapy regimen for unresectable PDAC and justify its use.
